source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) Minimum description length revisited
finding: Rissanen 1978 coined MDL and introduced the two-part code for parametric models. The two-part code is the oldest 'universal distribution'. The core idea: give each model one universal code, pick the model whose code gives the data the shortest length, plus a code for the model index.
numbers: Selection rule (1): minimise -log pi(model) - log p_bar_model(data). Universal codes named: Bayes mixture, NML (Shtarkov 1987), two-part, prequential plug-in (Rissanen 1984, Dawid 1984), switch, RIPr.
quote: MDL was introduced in 1978 by Jorma Rissanen in his paper Modeling by the Shortest Data Description
limits: Review by the original book author, so favourable to MDL. Everything is stated for probabilistic models with a defined likelihood.
agent_relevance: S7 tie-break: compare candidates by one total length, fit plus complexity, in the same units. The tie-break is only as good as the code used for each candidate.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) Minimum description length revisited
finding: NML (Shtarkov) distribution is the minimax-regret universal code: it spreads probability so that the worst-case extra bits over the best-fitting member of the model are smallest. Its log normaliser is the model complexity comp(M). Model choice = fit term + comp term.
numbers: Eq (6): choose model minimising -log p(data | MLE) - log v(MLE) + comp(M;v). For Bernoulli, comp = log of sum over n1 of C(n,n1)(n1/n)^n1(n0/n)^n0, within a constant of (1/2) log n.
limits: NML with flat luckiness is undefined for most models on unbounded outcome spaces (e.g. the normal location family). This forced the 'luckiness function' generalisation. Computing comp is hard for rich models.
agent_relevance: Shows the exact price of flexibility: a model that can fit any data pays a large comp term. A scaffold candidate (a program, a rule) that can fit anything has high complexity even if it fits the examples. This is the formal form of guardrail G3.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) Minimum description length revisited
finding: Asymptotic expansion: comp(M) = (k/2) log(n/2pi) + log of the integral of sqrt(det Fisher information) + o(1). Rissanen 1996 proved it for restricted parameter sets; Myung et al. 2000 gave it a geometric reading (volume of the model); Suzuki and Yamanishi 2018 proved the general case with nonuniform luckiness, solving open problem 6 of the 2007 book.
numbers: Penalty = (k/2) log n for k parameters, plus a model-geometry term that BIC drops. Bayes with Jeffreys prior matches NML up to o(1) for exponential families.
limits: Regularity conditions needed (exponential or curved-exponential families, restricted parameter set). Fails or needs repair for singular models such as neural nets and mixtures.
agent_relevance: BIC-style cost 'half log n bits per parameter' is a usable cheap proxy when counting candidate complexity, but it ignores how parameters are arranged.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) Minimum description length revisited
finding: The AIC versus BIC dilemma: MDL and Bayes factors act like BIC (consistent, but prediction-suboptimal by about a log n factor). Cross-validation acts like AIC (prediction-optimal, not consistent). Yang 2005 showed no method gets both. The switch distribution (Van Erven et al. 2007) gets strong consistency and loses only a log log n factor in prediction.
numbers: Prediction rates differ by a factor of order log n between BIC-type and AIC-type selection; the switch distribution loses an order log log n factor.
limits: Asymptotic statements for a finite model list. Constants not given. The result says nothing about small n with rich models.
agent_relevance: When the aim is a good final answer (prediction), not recovering the 'true' hypothesis, a compression tie-break can be too conservative. Keep a held-out check (S4/S8) alongside it.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) Minimum description length revisited
finding: MDL and Bayes can be inconsistent under misspecification, when all candidate models are wrong but one is best in KL divergence. First shown by Grunwald and Langford 2007 (artificial case with countably infinite model set), then Grunwald and van Ommen 2017 (linear regression with heteroskedastic noise), and De Heide 2016 on real data. Root cause: the no-hypercompression inequality holds against the true distribution only if the model contains it.
numbers: With a countable model set, MDL selects a suboptimal model for all large n. With a finite set, it may pick arbitrarily bad submodels at fairly large n. Fix: generalised likelihood p^eta with eta<1 (learning rate).
limits: The fix is proven for Bayesian-type universal codes. Real-data demonstrations are few.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant: our candidates are always misspecified. The shortest-description candidate can be wrong even with lots of data. Another reason compression must not be the only selector (G3, G5).

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) Minimum description length revisited
finding: Link to deep learning (section 6.4): networks that fit training data perfectly can still generalise. MDL-style explanation: flat minima need fewer bits to describe (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997; Hinton and van Camp 1993). Here MDL is used indirectly: compressibility of data given the learned weights implies generalisation (PAC-Bayes-style bounds).
numbers: Qualitative section. No single headline figure.
limits: Authors call this use less direct than hunting for the shortest description. Flatness measures are not invariant to reparameterisation (not discussed in the review).
agent_relevance: Supports the view that the right complexity for a neural scorer is the information in its weights, not its parameter count.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) Minimum description length revisited
finding: Luckiness functions replace priors and penalties. The v-MDL estimator argmax p_theta(data) v(theta) is penalised maximum likelihood and equals MAP if v is a density. Choice of v is like choosing a prior but v need not integrate. A data-driven default: set aside the first few outcomes and use them to fix v.
numbers: Eq (5): theta_hat_v = argmin { -log p_theta(data) - [-log v(theta)] }.
limits: The choice of v is subjective, same as a Bayesian prior; Grunwald and Roos say it cannot be avoided.
agent_relevance: Our prior over which candidate is simpler (shorter program, fewer free parameters) is a luckiness function. Make it explicit and fixed before seeing data (G3).

source: Grunwald (2004) A tutorial introduction to the minimum description length principle
finding: Founding story and the two versions. Crude MDL picks the hypothesis H minimising L(H)+L(D|H). It is arbitrary because L(H) depends on the coding scheme. Refined MDL uses one universal code for each model, so stochastic complexity = L(D | best fit) + COMP(H) and nothing is arbitrary.
numbers: Polynomial example: degree-k polynomial fitted to a small sample; line underfits, degree n-1 overfits, third degree wins on code length. Four interpretations of refined MDL: counting/geometric, two-part, Bayesian (Jeffreys prior), prequential.
limits: Tutorial; no experiments. The abstract says MDL automatically guards against overfitting, but section 2.10 lists conceptual problems.
agent_relevance: S7 should use the refined form: a fixed, pre-registered code for each candidate class, not a free-hand estimate of how complex a candidate looks.

source: Grunwald (2004) A tutorial introduction to the minimum description length principle
finding: Origins. Kolmogorov (1965), Chaitin (1969), Solomonoff (1964) gave the idea that regularity means compressibility, and the invariance theorem says program length changes only by a constant between universal languages. Rissanen 1978 was inspired by Kolmogorov and Akaike. Wallace and Boulton 1968 (MML) found a related idea independently without knowing Kolmogorov complexity. Prequential codes came with Rissanen 1984 and Dawid 1984.
numbers: Dates: Wallace-Boulton 1968; Rissanen 1978; Wallace-Freeman 1987; Rissanen 1996 (Fisher information and stochastic complexity).
limits: The invariance constant can be huge for short data, which is why ideal MDL gives no guidance on small samples (the tutorial states this).
agent_relevance: Different formalisms (MDL, MML, Solomonoff) agree on the principle but differ on the code; for small problems the choice of code decides the winner.

source: Grunwald (2004) A tutorial introduction to the minimum description length principle
finding: Bayes link. The Laplace-type expansion gives -log P_Bayes(x^n) - [-log P(x^n | theta_hat)] = (k/2) log n - log w(theta_hat) + (1/2) log|I(theta_hat)| + o(1). With Jeffreys prior w proportional to sqrt|I|, refined NML selection becomes indistinguishable from Bayes factor selection.
numbers: Same expansion as Schwarz 1978 (BIC) when only the k/2 log n term is kept. Example 2.19: plug-in with raw ML estimator gives infinite code length after data (0,0,1); adding one virtual 0 and one virtual 1 (Laplace) repairs it.
limits: The equivalence is asymptotic and for regular models only.
agent_relevance: Practical lesson for prequential scoring of candidates: never let a scorer assign probability zero to an unseen case; smooth it (Laplace). Otherwise one miss gives infinite cost.

source: Hinton and van Camp (1993) Keeping neural networks simple by minimizing the description length of the weights
finding: First MDL treatment of neural networks. Weights get Gaussian noise; the noise level is adapted to trade expected squared error against the information in the weights. The bits-back argument shows the cost of sending noisy weights is the KL divergence between posterior and prior, not the full precision cost.
numbers: Exact derivatives of expected squared error and weight information are given for one hidden layer of nonlinear units with linear outputs. Quantised-weight coding rejected because cost has no smooth derivative.
quote: Supervised neural networks generalize well if there is much less information in the weights than in the output vectors
limits: Tested on small problems in 1993. Variational codes were later found weak as compression bounds (see Blier and Ollivier 2018).
agent_relevance: The ancestor of variational and prequential neural description lengths. Gives the principle: information in the weights counts as part of the description.

source: Blier and Ollivier (2018) The description length of deep learning models
finding: Two-part code with float32 weights is far worse than the plain uniform code. The prequential (online) code beats variational codes by a large margin, so deep nets do compress data when parameter cost is counted properly.
numbers: Float32 two-part: 32 Mbits for a 1M-parameter model, about 200x the uniform code on CIFAR-10. MNIST labels: uniform log2(10) per label; variational 24.1 kbits (ratio 0.12, test acc 95.5%); best prequential CNN 4.10 kbits (ratio 0.021, test acc 99.5%), 6x shorter than variational. CIFAR-10: variational 89.0 kbits (ratio 0.54, acc 61.6%); prequential VGG with augmentation and batch norm 45.3 kbits (ratio 0.27, acc about 93%); with switching 34.6 kbits.
limits: Lower bounds on code length; only labels given inputs are coded. Prequential cost needs training at many data sizes (expensive). Authors say variational results may reflect the particular variational method used.
agent_relevance: Prequential coding is the practical, cheap MDL: score a candidate by how well it predicts the next case after learning from the earlier ones. This is exactly an S4/S7 test that needs no held-out set beyond the sequence itself.

source: Blier and Ollivier (2018) The description length of deep learning models
finding: Random labels cannot be compressed. Networks reach 100% train accuracy on random labels (Zhang et al. 2017) but the description length stays at the uniform code, and there is no information in the weights. Real labels have about half their code in the weights.
numbers: Fig 1: MNIST, MLP 3x200 ReLU. True labels: code below uniform, about half of it in the weights. Fake labels: code converges to uniform (log2 10 bits per label), no mutual information between input and output.
limits: One model, one dataset; an illustration of the principle, not a statistical test.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of G3: fitting the given examples proves nothing. A candidate that memorises the examples has no compression. Measure code length including the candidate itself.

source: Blier and Ollivier (2018) The description length of deep learning models
finding: Catch-up phenomenon: a large model overfits when it has seen little data, so its cumulative prequential code is worse than uniform for a long time, even after per-label cost is below uniform. Switching between models (Van Erven et al.) fixes much of it.
numbers: CIFAR-10 VGGb: per-label cost drops below uniform after about 1,000 samples, but the cumulative ratio stays above 1 until about 5,000 samples. Switching between models with different stopping times saved over 11 kbits.
limits: The remedy needs several candidate models and a switching rule; adds compute.
agent_relevance: At small sample counts (a few examples in a prompt) rich candidates cost more than simple ones. A tie-break by total length favours simple candidates early, which matches G12 (spend where there is a foothold).

source: Voita and Titov (2020) Information-theoretic probing with minimum description length
finding: MDL probes replace probe accuracy with the code length of the labels given a frozen representation. Two codes are used: variational (Bayesian compression) and online. They agree on trends and are stable across settings and seeds, while accuracy is not.
numbers: Part-of-speech on Penn Treebank (train 39,832 sentences, 950,028 targets). In a ten-setting test, accuracy gave the wrong verdict (control task beat linguistic task) in 8 of 10 settings; MDL was right in 10 of 10. Layer 0: control-task accuracy higher but code twice as long as the linguistic task.
limits: Linguistic probing tasks; verdicts judged against the known control task. They note Blier and Ollivier found variational codes poor on images, whereas here both codes agree.
agent_relevance: Evidence that code length separates real structure from memorisation better than accuracy on the same data. A tie-break by code length is more stable than by accuracy.

source: Voita and Titov (2020) Information-theoretic probing with minimum description length
finding: Model cost reveals complexity. For the real task the best probe is small and sparse (33 to 75 neurons in layers 2 and 3 after pruning); for random-label control tasks it needs several times more model code. Seed noise flips accuracy rankings (layers 1 and 2: 97.48 vs 97.31 for seed 1, 97.38 vs 97.48 for seed 0) while code-length rankings stay separated.
numbers: Embedding layer code about twice as long as layer 1. Control task codelengths at least twice the linguistic ones. Starting probe 1024-1000-1000 pruned to e.g. 664-55-35 (layer 1 linguistic) versus 824-272-260 (control).
limits: Penn Treebank POS only for the detailed numbers; seven further tasks (constituents, dependencies, entities, SRL, coreference, relations) reported with random-representation baselines.
agent_relevance: Report model cost and data cost separately. A candidate answer that needs a long, ad-hoc justification is a memoriser; the split shows it.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language modeling is compression
finding: Language models are lossless compressors via arithmetic coding, with code length equal to the log loss. Large text-trained LLMs beat domain compressors on images and audio they were not trained on.
numbers: Chinchilla 70B compresses ImageNet patches to 43.4% of raw size (PNG 58.5%) and LibriSpeech to 16.4% (FLAC 30.3%). enwik9 raw rate Chinchilla 70B 8.3%, gzip 32.3%.
limits: Raw rate excludes model size. With parameters counted (adjusted rate, two-part code at 2 bytes per parameter) big models lose except on TB-scale data. Possible training-set leakage of encoded images is noted as unlikely.
agent_relevance: Gives a direct way to get a data-given-hypothesis term from the model itself, and to see that ordinary log loss ignores the hypothesis cost. Our S7 should not use a big model's loss alone as the complexity measure.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language modeling is compression
finding: Scaling laws look different once model size is counted: adjusted compression rate has a minimum at a model size that depends on the data size. Larger models win on larger datasets and lose on smaller ones. Simpler tokenisers compress better for small transformers.
numbers: Vanilla Transformers trained on enwik8, tested on enwik7, enwik8 and enwik9; model size = 2 bytes per parameter. Adjusted rate rises again past a critical size for each dataset. Compressing float16 weights further with gzip or LZMA2 only reaches 92.2% and 89.1% of size on a 38M-parameter model.
limits: Offline two-part accounting, small models. Prequential accounting would be kinder to large models (the authors note).
agent_relevance: Same size-versus-data trade-off holds for how complex a candidate may be given how few examples we have. With 3 to 5 examples only very simple candidates can be justified by compression.

source: Gruenwald and Langford (2007) Suboptimal behavior of Bayes and MDL in classification under misspecification
finding: Proves that two-part MDL and Bayesian classifiers can be inconsistent: a learning problem exists where, for all amounts of data, the generalisation error of the MDL classifier stays bounded away from the best achievable error in the class.
numbers: Theorem 2 / Corollary 1: there is a countable classifier set C and a distribution D such that the MDL and Bayes classifiers stay at least K away from the best error in C. Requires priors with heavy tails. Holds for all large m.
limits: Authors warn: only some versions of MDL and Bayes are covered (two-part MDL for classification, classifiers turned into distributions by crossing with an error-rate prior). The case is artificial.
agent_relevance: The simplest-looking classifier or rule set can be systematically wrong when the true rule is outside the candidate class. Do not trust a compression tie-break when all candidates are likely wrong.

source: Gruenwald and van Ommen (2017) Inconsistency of Bayesian inference for misspecified linear models, and a proposal for repairing it
finding: Empirical demonstration in a plain regression setting: with heteroskedastic data and a homoskedastic model, the Bayes posterior puts mass on ever higher-dimensional models as n grows. SafeBayes learns a learning rate eta from the data (prequentially) and repairs it.
numbers: Model set M0..M50 polynomial basis. With 100 data points (about 50 at (0,0)), standard Bayes overfits; SafeBayes picked eta about 0.4 and matches the best predictor. eta=1 is standard Bayes; eta=0 leaves the posterior equal to the prior.
limits: Arxiv version 1 (2014) text read. The published version is shorter; one of four SafeBayes variants was uncompetitive. Synthetic data only.
agent_relevance: Shows that the same-model-wrong problem arises in a simple regression. A softer weighting of evidence (eta below 1) is a practical hedge: do not let a long run of fits swamp the choice.

source: Perez, Kiela and Cho (2021) Rissanen Data Analysis: Examining dataset characteristics via description length
finding: Rissanen Data Analysis (RDA): a capability or feature is useful for a dataset if adding it shortens the online code length of the labels. The estimate is interpreted only relative to other estimates with the same learner.
numbers: Word order on GLUE: MNLI labels compress to 50% of the label-prior baseline with word order versus 75% with shuffled words; CoLA labels cannot be compressed at all without word order. HotpotQA: subquestion decomposition reduces codelength mainly in high- and mid-loss regimes, not at full data.
limits: Estimates depend on the learner and the coding blocks. Only used for relative comparisons. Experiments on NLP datasets with pretrained models.
agent_relevance: A testable way to decide whether a helper (a reframing, a decomposition, an extra operator) earns its place: if it does not shorten the code, drop it. This is guardrail G7 in MDL form.

source: Wu, Wang, Ye and Kong (2023) Self-adaptive in-context learning: an information compression perspective
finding: Pick the in-context example set and order for each test input by an MDL-style score: the model's expected label code length under that prompt, with model cost ignored since the model is fixed. Gains over random choice are large; over similarity retrieval small.
numbers: GPT2-XL, 8 datasets, 3 seeds. Mean accuracy: TopK+MDL 60.16, TopK 58.14, random 42.78 (40% relative gain), TopK+LocalE 51.36, majority vote 50.43, MI selection 42.85. Lower mean MDL went with higher accuracy on 4 datasets (e.g. SST-2: TopK 0.6861 at 83.91% vs TopK+MDL 0.6810 at 91.51%).
limits: Their MDL is the entropy of the model's own output distribution (expected code length), so it favours confident prompts. Only 10 sampled orderings ranked; one small model; oracle choice still far above.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM use of the principle for S7. Note it is a confidence criterion, which G5 and G10 warn about: low entropy can mean confident but wrong. Use with a code-run check, not alone.

source: Huang, Zhang, Shan and He (2024) Compression represents intelligence linearly
finding: Across 31 public LLMs and 12 benchmarks, average benchmark score is nearly linear in bits per character on external text corpora, in three skill areas (knowledge and commonsense, coding, maths).
numbers: Pearson correlation about -0.95 per domain; overall -0.93 with RMSE 3.1% of the linear fit. Holds for most single benchmarks too.
limits: Correlation, not cause. Models from different families mixed. Not a statement about a single reasoning step.
agent_relevance: Supports using held-out predictive code length as a cheap quality signal across models, not across candidate answers for one problem.

source: Elmoznino, Marty, Kasetty, Gagnon, Mittal, Fathi, Sridhar and Lajoie (2025) In-context learning and Occam's razor
finding: Next-token loss over a context equals the prequential code length of that context, so in-context learning is trained to minimise training error plus the complexity of the model learned from context. This is MDL in disguise. A pretrained LLM did not minimise it on a hard task.
numbers: Averaged over 5 seeds; meta-training on 10,000 tasks of 1,000 points each; prequential ICL beats train-risk ICL at short contexts on all tasks and the gap grows with task difficulty; L2-regularised SGD baselines also lose in low-data regimes. On the Mastermind task a large pretrained LLM had a longer prequential code than a naive empirical-marginal predictor.
limits: Synthetic tasks, small transformers and Mamba; architecture matters (only the plain Transformer did well on Mastermind, SSMs on the HMM task). Underfitting is a noted weakness.
agent_relevance: Says why simple hypotheses should win with little context. Warns that a general LLM is not guaranteed to follow the Occam preference on a new task: compute the compression in code.

source: Lotfi, Finzi, Kuang, Rudner, Goldblum and Wilson (2024) Non-vacuous generalization bounds for large language models
finding: First non-vacuous compression-based generalisation bounds for pretrained LLMs, using SubLoRA (LoRA plus a random subspace) to make the model description short enough. Larger models gave better bounds and were more compressible.
numbers: GPT-2 124M, OpenWebText, document-level bits-per-dimension bound: SubLoRA 12.12, LoRA 13.09, subspace 14.59, original model 70.76 (vacuous), random guess 15.62. Top-1 error bound 96.41% (random guess 99.99%). Validation BPD of the bound-optimal models: SubLoRA 10.53 versus original 4.35. Models up to 849M parameters still non-vacuous.
limits: Bounds are loose (BPD bound 12.12 vs validation 10.53); the compressed models are worse predictors than the original; gives guarantees on average per-document loss, not on any single answer.
agent_relevance: Shows that a hypothesis cost can be counted for an LLM and that the total can be small. It does not give per-answer scores, so for us it is background support for simple hypotheses generalise only.

source: Whitney, Song, Brandfonbrener, Altosaar and Cho (2020) Evaluating representations by the complexity of learning low-loss predictors
finding: Critique of MDL-style and validation-loss measures of representation quality: both depend on the evaluation set size, so rankings can flip as data grows. Proposed surplus description length (SDL) and epsilon sample complexity (SC), which fix the loss level instead of the data size.
numbers: MNIST with CIFAR-pretrained CNN features, raw pixels and VAE bottleneck; and ELMo layers on part-of-speech (4096-d vectors, 48k output space). In both, MDL and validation accuracy chose different representations at different evaluation-set sizes.
limits: Alternatives require training predictors to a loss target; results are measured, not proven to dominate.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition on S7 tie-breaks: with a small sample, code-length rankings can reverse when more data arrive. Prefer a rule that says insufficient data over a forced pick.
